st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-redesign thesis and materially extends it by identifying intrapreneurs as the actors who convert AI capabilities into new professional workflows. It also adds a controlled-adoption argument: organisations should govern existing employee use rather than merely delay deployment, while treating confidentiality through enterprise configuration and context-specific exceptions.
qs: The intrapreneurs are the people who see that expansion and build workflows around it before their competitors or employers do.
It's that their people are already using it without any controls at all.

st.t: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
st.an: The source accepts that legal subject matter and later delivery to counsel do not create privilege, distinguishes independent consumer use from counsel-directed work, and materially extends the proposition by identifying contractual data protections and access controls as practical confidentiality safeguards while not claiming they automatically establish privilege.
qs: This sounds obvious, but the implication is precise: communications with an AI tool are not attorney-client communications, even if the topic is legal strategy and even if you later hand the output to your attorney.
And it's one with a straightforward solution: enterprise agreements, which restrict data use, prohibit training on your inputs, and support proper access controls.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core case that AI should enable new workflows and capabilities rather than merely accelerate inherited tasks. It materially extends the implementation argument by identifying intrapreneurs as workflow builders and uncontrolled employee use as a reason for governed enterprise adoption, while offering little direct evidence on pricing or apprenticeship.
qs: The intrapreneurs are the people who see that expansion and build workflows around it before their competitors or employers do.
It's that their people are already using it without any controls at all.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s account of procedure-based differentiation by showing how a lawyer encoded firm-specific review and negotiation practices into reusable Claude skills, then corrected and refined them before packaging them as a Cowork plugin. It offers a concrete implementation example, while making no measured performance claim or case for autonomous legal practice.
qs: How we approach contract review from the client's perspective, not just spotting issues but building negotiation strategy.
I pushed back on two of the suggestions—one was too broad, one we handle differently than the default approach.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-reconfiguration framing and materially extends it: AI can enable previously impractical forms of analysis, not merely accelerate existing tasks, while workflow-building intrapreneurs and controlled enterprise deployment are organisational complements needed to capture that value. It also adds that unmanaged employee use may pose a greater near-term risk than formal adoption, though it gives limited attention to verification and apprenticeship risks.
qs: She's doing something no associate in the firm's history has ever done: longitudinal pattern analysis across the firm's entire institutional memory, as a byproduct of finishing the normal work in a fraction of the time.
It's that their people are already using it without any controls at all.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts AI as an operating-model transformation and materially extends the cluster by arguing that redesigned workflows can make previously impractical analytical work feasible, rather than merely accelerating existing tasks. It also reinforces controlled enterprise adoption by identifying unmanaged employee use as a key organisational risk.
qs: She's doing something no associate in the firm's history has ever done: longitudinal pattern analysis across the firm's entire institutional memory, as a byproduct of finishing the normal work in a fraction of the time.
The intrapreneurs are the people who see that expansion and build workflows around it before their competitors or employers do.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s lifecycle-confidentiality proposition by showing how privilege and confidentiality turn on who directs the AI, the user’s professional capacity, and the platform’s contractual data practices. It adds a practical distinction between consumer and enterprise terms while cautioning that discoverability is not equivalent to loss of business confidentiality.
qs: The distinction is who's directing the tool and in what capacity.
And it's one with a straightforward solution: enterprise agreements, which restrict data use, prohibit training on your inputs, and support proper access controls.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s significance lies in new capabilities and workflow redesign rather than task speed alone. It extends the cluster by identifying intrapreneurs as organisational actors who convert capability gains into early, controlled workflows, while not directly resolving pricing or market-wide value capture.
qs: AI expands the frontier of what's possible at a given cost.
The intrapreneurs are the people who see that expansion and build workflows around it before their competitors or employers do.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, governed deployment and materially extends the cluster’s operating-model argument by identifying bottom-up intrapreneurs as workflow builders who translate AI capabilities into repeatable organizational practice. It also adds a concrete governance rationale for sanctioned enterprise adoption over bans that drive use into unmanaged tools.
qs: The intrapreneurs are the people who see that expansion and build workflows around it before their competitors or employers do.
The alternative: sanctioned enterprise tools, proper data handling agreements, clear usage policies, training.

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition by providing a first-person example of Claude moving beyond generic model access into firm-specific legal workflows that can be refined, packaged and distributed through Claude Cowork. It demonstrates the technical plausibility of provider-native workflow control, but does not assess vendor competition, displacement, productivity or legal accuracy.
qs: It didn't suggest "draft emails faster" or "summarize documents." It identified specific things that my law firm, @rainsllp , does repeatedly, in specific ways: how we structure engagement letters for startup clients.
An hour later, we had a refined set, and I bundled them into a single plugin for Claude Cowork (Anthropic's agent mode inside the Claude Desktop app).

kp.k: Intrapreneurs turn individual judgment into organizational infrastructure
kp.d: Shapiro argues that professionals can encode domain expertise in AI-enabled workflows, secure colleagues' adoption, and scale their judgment within existing organizations. He frames this as internal entrepreneurship rather than simply personal task automation, predicting substantial career opportunities for early builders.
qs: By "intrapreneur" I mean the person inside an existing organization who builds AI-enabled workflows, gets them adopted, and turns individual judgment into repeatable systems.
It's about what happens when expertise becomes infrastructure.

kp.k: A practitioner describes packaging legal expertise into Claude skills
kp.d: Shapiro reports building a plugin in three hours using Anthropic's 33-page skills guide and Claude's analysis of his chat history. The workflows covered startup engagement letters, client-centered contract review and negotiation strategy, documentation memos, and legal track changes. He describes refining the suggestions through domain-specific pushback before bundling them for Claude Cowork; this is a personal implementation account, not a measured study of effectiveness.
qs: I put it all into a plugin last month. In three hours.
I pushed back on two of the suggestions—one was too broad, one we handle differently than the default approach.
A skill is a structured set of instructions that tells Claude how to behave in a specific context.

kp.k: Reusable expertise could standardize practice with less senior supervision
kp.d: Using hypothetical firms of 50, 500, and 5,000 people, Shapiro argues that shared plugins could give associates access to senior analytical frameworks without lengthy training sessions or supervision that consumes senior time. His proposed benefit is scalable standardization and quality control, not merely speed; the examples do not report actual firm-wide deployment outcomes or changes in associate-to-partner ratios.
qs: Every associate who opens Claude for a client matter would have access to the same analytical frameworks, the same standards, the same approach to structuring advice that I've spent over a decade of my own practice developing.
Not through supervision that consumes senior time. Through a plugin.
Once you've turned your judgment or expertise into reusable artifacts, you can scale it across a whole team with almost no marginal training cost.

kp.k: Large organizations offer greater internal scaling opportunities
kp.d: Shapiro contrasts small organizations' low bureaucracy and immediate feedback with large institutions that have already purchased AI platforms but lack sophisticated workflow builders. He predicts larger aggregate gains and career rewards for people who close this implementation gap. His example of two thousand people becoming twenty percent more productive is illustrative rather than an observed result.
qs: But there's an enormous gap between having access to AI and knowing what to do with it.
It's that two thousand people become twenty percent more productive partly because of something you figured out.
You don't have to implement anything at scale personally. You write the playbook and it spreads.

kp.k: The strategic opportunity is new capabilities, not faster tasks
kp.d: Shapiro argues that lower analysis costs enable previously uneconomical services and revenue opportunities. His financial-analysis example involves synthesizing ten thousand earnings calls; his legal example imagines reducing a 40,000-document review from two weeks to four hours, then analyzing five years of deals to find structures associated with indemnification disputes 18 months after closing. These scenarios illustrate his proposed mechanism, rather than documented productivity findings.
qs: There's a meaningful distinction between doing existing tasks faster and expanding what can be done at all, at a given cost.
The old job: read 40,000 documents in a data room over two weeks, flag issues, summarize findings.

She's doing something no associate in the firm's history has ever done: longitudinal pattern analysis across the firm's entire institutional memory, as a byproduct of finishing the normal work in a fraction of the time.

kp.k: Low adoption supports an early-mover thesis
kp.d: Shapiro uses John LeFevre's global adoption chart to argue that AI remains early in its diffusion: roughly 6.8 billion nonusers, about 1.3 billion free chatbot users, and 2 to 5 million coding-level users. LeFevre's embedded post states that 84% have never used AI and 0.3% of users pay for premium services. Shapiro explicitly discourages precision-focused scrutiny and compares the chart with the internet in 1995 and mobile in 2005; the resulting opportunity claim is an analogy and prediction, not evidence of legal-sector adoption rates.
qs: Don't nitpick the exact numbers; look at the shape.
84% of people have never used AI, and just 0.3% of users pay for premium services.
The internet in 1995 looked like this. Mobile in 2005 looked like this.
The red dots, people using coding-level AI, are 2 to 5 million on a planet of eight billion.

kp.k: Reported privilege ruling distinguishes client-directed consumer AI use
kp.d: Shapiro reports that United States v. Heppner, identified in the notes as a February 17, 2026 S.D.N.Y. ruling by Judge Rakoff, denied attorney-client privilege and work-product protection to roughly thirty reports generated independently by a criminal defendant using free consumer Claude and subsequently shared with counsel. He emphasizes that legal discussion with AI is not attorney-client communication and argues that lawyer-directed AI use occupies a different posture; he does not report a ruling establishing protection for that different scenario.
qs: roughly thirty "AI reports" a defendant generated with the free consumer version of Claude were not protected by attorney-client privilege or the work-product doctrine.
communications with an AI tool are not attorney-client communications, even if the topic is legal strategy and even if you later hand the output to your attorney.
The distinction is who's directing the tool and in what capacity.

kp.d: In Shapiro's account of Heppner, consumer terms allowing prompt review, data retention, and disclosure under legal process defeated a reasonable expectation of confidentiality. He presents enterprise agreements restricting data use, prohibiting training, and supporting access controls as a solution, and attributes to Debevoise the view that different enterprise terms should receive different treatment. He separately distinguishes litigation discoverability from confidentiality sufficient for business purposes.
qs: Judge Rakoff found that Heppner had no reasonable expectation of confidentiality because the consumer terms of service for Claude explicitly reserve the right to review prompts, retain data, and disclose to government authorities under legal process.
Debevoise's analysis of the opinion makes this point explicitly, that enterprise AI tools operating under different contractual terms should be treated differently.
The fact that information could be subpoenaed or discovered in litigation doesn't mean it isn't sufficiently confidential for other (business) purposes.

kp.k: Enterprise adoption requires contracts and internal controls
kp.d: Shapiro recommends enterprise Claude or ChatGPT for most professional applications. He describes OpenAI's business terms as limiting content use and barring model improvement without opt-in, and Anthropic's commercial privacy materials as providing the same default. Both offer DPAs; some vendors support HIPAA-ready deployments through a BAA in the appropriate enterprise SKU. His comparison with ordinary cloud-system risks is conditional on appropriate configuration, paperwork, and controls, with exceptions for extraordinarily sensitive information.
qs: Both offer DPAs, and some vendors offer HIPAA-ready deployments via a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) in the right enterprise SKU—but you need the paperwork in place, and you still need internal controls.
The core questions are contracts, access controls, retention, auditability, and who can review content under what circumstances.
For most professional applications, enterprise versions of Anthropic Claude or OpenAI ChatGPT are the right answer.

kp.k: Bans risk pushing AI use outside organizational governance
kp.d: Shapiro argues that prohibiting AI without a sanctioned alternative makes use less visible rather than stopping it. He cites UpGuard as finding about 80% of surveyed employees using unapproved AI, with similar numbers among security leaders, and IBM as finding about $670,000 higher breach costs in organizations with high shadow AI levels than those with low or none. He recommends enterprise tools, data-handling agreements, usage policies, and training; the reported cost comparison is not presented as a study proving that bans cause breaches.
qs: If you prohibit AI use without providing a sanctioned alternative, you don't stop AI use. You just stop knowing about it.
UpGuard's "Shadow AI" research found about 80% of surveyed employees using unapproved AI at work, and, awkwardly, similar numbers among security leaders.
IBM found organizations with high shadow AI levels saw about $670,000 higher breach costs than those with low or none.

kp.k: Local models trade capability for infrastructure control
kp.d: Shapiro recommends considering locally run models for genuinely sensitive trade secrets, major litigation strategy, and nonpublic M&A terms. He claims local models are currently one to three generations behind frontier models and require infrastructure investment and maintenance while lacking seamless synchronization. His suggestion that enterprise cloud tools suit the other 95% of organizational work is a qualified judgment rather than a reported measurement.
qs: Running an LLM locally means the model operates on hardware you control. Nothing leaves your infrastructure.
Models available for local deployment are currently one to three generations behind frontier models.
For the other 95% of what your organization does, enterprise cloud tools are (probably) the right answer.

kp.k: Unsupervised agents combine dangerous read and write permissions
kp.d: Shapiro describes OpenClaw as a multistep, tool-using agent framework and argues that combining sensitive-data access with unsupervised email, posting, and code execution is presently too risky for most organizations. He cites Cisco findings on malicious skills exfiltrating data and prompt injection redirecting agents, and reports a February Moltbook security hole exposing over a million credentials. He predicts eventual improvements through isolation, permission models, and vetted skills, while treating current capabilities as ahead of security architecture.
qs: Read access to everything sensitive in your organization, plus write access to the internet, in a single tool that runs unsupervised is, needless to say, a security nightmare that speaks for itself.
Cisco researchers found that malicious skills could exfiltrate data and that prompt-injection attacks could steer agent behavior without the user realizing it.
OpenClaw-style autonomous agents: promising and too risky right now, in that order.

kp.k: Domain experts must verify outputs before scaling workflows
kp.d: Shapiro recommends inventorying actual work, identifying newly feasible analyses, encoding judgment, and piloting within the builder's sphere of expertise. He explicitly assigns human quality control to the domain expert, who must distinguish correct from merely plausible output, catch subtle errors, and fix edge cases before broader rollout. This qualifies his earlier claims about readily scalable expertise: local validation remains necessary.
qs: You need to be the quality-control layer, because right now you're the only person who can tell whether the output is actually right or just plausible.
Your first version will misfire on edge cases.
Treat this phase as R&D, not deployment. Find product-market fit first. Then ship.

kp.k: Measure outcomes and spread demonstrated workflows internally
kp.d: Shapiro urges builders to track turnaround time, error rates, and iterations before client readiness, rather than relying on perceived speed. His twelve-versus-four contract example with unchanged client feedback is an illustrative internal business case, not a reported result. He recommends documenting outcomes to generate colleague demand, predicting successful adoption will originate with a few effective builders rather than top-down mandates.
qs: Track turnaround time, error rates, iterations before a deliverable is client-ready.
"I reviewed twelve contracts in the time it used to take me to review four, and client feedback scores didn't drop" is the kind of sentence that moves budgets.
The organizations that figure this out won't do it through top-down mandate, they'll do it because one or two people built something that worked and everyone else wanted it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shapiro argues that AI enables lawyers to turn individual professional judgment into reusable organizational systems, expand the services they can economically provide, and gain career advantages by building workflows that colleagues adopt.
pts.d: Shapiro reports packaging his own legal know-how into a Claude plugin in three hours. He argues that reusable skills can distribute established approaches to engagement letters, client-centered contract review, negotiation strategy, advice documentation and legal edits across a firm, improving standardization and quality control while reducing dependence on senior supervision and repeated training. His hypothetical scaling from 50 to 500 or 5,000 lawyers is a claim about potential organizational deployment, not a reported rollout. He predicts especially large rewards for internal workflow builders in large organizations that have bought enterprise AI but lack sophisticated users. His example of 2,000 people becoming 20% more productive is illustrative, not a measured result. Beyond efficiency, he claims AI makes previously uneconomical analysis and new services possible. His document-review scenario contrasts reviewing 40,000 documents over two weeks with a four-hour AI-enabled review, followed by analysis of five years of deals to identify patterns associated with later indemnification disputes. This is presented as a capability illustration rather than an identified client matter or study. He makes parallel claims for finance, consulting and healthcare administration. On governance, he argues that properly configured enterprise AI generally offers a risk profile comparable to established cloud services, whereas bans encourage uncontrolled consumer-tool use. He distinguishes client-directed consumer AI use from lawyer-directed use and argues that enterprise contractual protections matter to confidentiality and privilege analysis. He recommends local models for exceptionally sensitive work and considers broadly permissioned autonomous agents too risky for most organizations at present.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines Shapiro's personal plugin-building experience, hypothetical productivity scenarios, cited adoption and security research, and his interpretation of legal and vendor-contract materials; it does not report measured results from a firm-wide implementation.
pts.d: The principal experiential basis is Shapiro's account of using Anthropic's skills guide and his Claude chat history to identify recurring workflows at Rains LLP, revising suggestions and bundling them into a Claude Cowork plugin. He describes encoding over a decade of practice experience but supplies no before-and-after quality or productivity results for that plugin. The 40,000-document review, retrospective deal analysis, 2,000-person productivity gain and twelve-versus-four contract review example are illustrations rather than documented outcomes. He uses a global adoption chart quoted from John LeFevre to support his own early-adopter opportunity thesis, explicitly deemphasizing precise numerical accuracy; these are not legal-sector adoption data. For governance, he cites UpGuard's finding of approximately 80% unapproved AI use among surveyed employees and IBM's approximately $670,000 higher breach costs in organizations with high shadow-AI levels. He uses those findings to argue for controlled adoption; they do not constitute a reported test of AI bans in law firms. His privilege discussion relies on his account of United States v. Heppner and a Debevoise analysis, distinguishing a defendant's independent consumer-Claude use from attorney-directed work and differently contracted enterprise tools. He also invokes OpenAI and Anthropic enterprise terms and privacy materials, DPAs and conditional BAA availability. His agent-risk claims draw on Cisco research concerning malicious skills and prompt injection, plus reported OpenClaw/Moltbook incidents. The notes cite the BCG field experiment, but the article does not state its findings or use a specific result to substantiate the legal-work examples.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Shapiro presents workflow building and expanded analytical capabilities as available now in 2026, predicts a decade of opportunity for early internal adopters, and conditions responsible scaling on domain expertise, local testing, human verification and appropriate governance.
pts.d: The article describes the plugin as built the previous month and prototypes as possible within an hour or evening. Shapiro's career prediction concerns the coming decade, while his claims about sparse sophisticated use and institutional opportunity concern the present. Organizational benefits depend on a knowledgeable practitioner encoding sound approaches, securing actual adoption and testing the workflow before broad rollout. Despite his claims about reduced training and supervision requirements at scale, his implementation advice explicitly requires the builder to check whether output is correct rather than merely plausible, catch subtle errors and edge cases, iterate, and measure turnaround time, error rates and revisions before client readiness. Enterprise-cloud recommendations are qualified by proper configuration, contractual protections, access controls, retention, auditability, data-handling policies and training. He excludes exceptionally sensitive material, including active M&A terms, major litigation strategy and genuine trade secrets, from his general cloud recommendation. For those cases, local models may be appropriate, but he describes current local offerings as one to three generations behind frontier models and requiring infrastructure and maintenance. He predicts agent security architecture will eventually improve without specifying when; current unsupervised agents with extensive read and external write permissions are, in his view, unsuitable for most organizations. His statement that enterprise cloud tools suit the other 95% of organizational work is expressly qualified as probable and is not supported by a reported workload measurement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main beneficiaries in Shapiro's account are domain-expert workflow builders and their organizations, with distinct implications for associates, senior lawyers, boutique and major firms, clients, and governance teams.
pts.d: Experienced lawyers can distribute their analytical frameworks through reusable tools rather than only through individual advice, training or supervision. Associates can access those frameworks and, in Shapiro's scenario, move beyond document processing into firm-wide longitudinal analysis that informs partners about recurring deal risks. He does not predict associate headcount reductions, changes to staffing shapes, billing-model changes or lawyer replacement. Startup clients are the immediate context for his own encoded workflows; their proposed benefits concern more consistent client-centered review, negotiation advice, engagement documentation and advice records, rather than demonstrated fee reductions. Small firms and startups have an adoption advantage because they face less bureaucracy and can obtain feedback quickly. Major law firms and other large institutions offer greater potential aggregate gains because a workflow can reach many colleagues, especially where enterprise tools are already available but underused. Internal builders gain career visibility and influence by delivering measurable outcomes and securing adoption. Compliance, security and organizational leadership are affected by the need to govern actual employee use rather than rely on bans. Clients and organizations handling exceptionally sensitive information face different deployment choices from routine enterprise users. Across other information-intensive professions, Shapiro predicts new analytical products and capabilities rather than only faster completion of existing work.
